Displacement

/dis-PLAYS-ment/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Displacement means the act of moving something from its usual place or position; the forced removal of people from their home.

The museum's renovation meant the temporary displacement of every sculpture in the east wing to a warehouse across town.

Worked Example

The wildfire caused the displacement of thousands of residents, who spent weeks in shelters far from home.

The residents did not choose to move — the fire forced them out of the place where they belonged. That concrete, forced removal of people or things from their usual place is displacement, the word's most serious real-world use.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

uprooting: Uprooting is tearing someone or something out of the place where it has grown established, the way a tree loses its ground, and it stresses the wrench of the tearing. Displacement is the cooler, formal word for the same forced removal — the term reports, courts, and agencies use.

dislocation: A dislocation is a jolt out of joint or proper order — a shoulder slips its socket, an economy is thrown out of balance. Displacement means being forced out of a place altogether. Something dislocated is still there, just wrongly arranged; something displaced has been pushed out entirely.

expulsion: An expulsion is a forcing-out performed by an authority with the power to eject — a school expels a student, a country expels a diplomat. Displacement needs no expeller: a storm or a demolition crew can displace people. Expulsion is a ruling someone hands down; displacement is a condition events create.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

anchoring: fixing something firmly in its place

homecoming: a return to one's own place

Where it sits · how forced and permanent the uprooting is — shift → displacement → exile

shift vs. displacement: A shift is a small, often voluntary change of position; displacement means being pushed out of your place.

exile vs. displacement: Exile is stronger than displacement — a forced removal from your homeland with no permission to return.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: apart, away

Root — place

Root — place: a spot or position (from platea, 'broad street')

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Dis- ('away') + place ('a spot or position') + -ment ('act or process of') spells the meaning out exactly: displacement is 'the process of being moved away from one's place.'

Use the root in a new word: misplace

Use the root in a new word: misplace: I always misplace my keys when I'm rushing out the door.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / journalistic

Displacement is concrete: something or someone is physically forced out of its usual place — news reports use it for people driven from their homes, and physics uses it for the water an object pushes aside. Keep it distinct from detriment, which names the abstract harm or disadvantage an action causes; displacement is the forced moving itself, not the damage that follows.
